preamble: Glottalization of [ʃ] by fusion with a following uvular stop. Beck (2000) shows that in Upper Necaxa Totonac Proto-Northern Totonac *q became a glottal stop and the resulting fricative + glottal stop sequences collapsed into ejective fricatives: *šq > *šʔ > šʼ (Beck writes š for [ʃ]). Upper Necaxa šʼ corresponds to šq in Apapantilla, Papantla and Zapotitlan Totonac, and Tlachichilco Tepehua also has šq in 'lizard, iguana'. The same change produced sʼ from *sq and ɬʼ from *ɬq. Fricative + ʔ sequences formed later across a morpheme boundary do not fuse: iš- '3SG.POSSESSIVE' + ʔoːlúː 'old man, husband' gives išʔoːlúː 'her husband', not *išʼoːlúː. Beck also notes that the Upper Necaxa ejective fricatives lower neighbouring vowels just as q does in the other languages. He describes the result, ejective fricatives with no ejective stops, as to his knowledge unique among the world's languages; Wikipedia, citing Beck (2006), confirms that *q became a glottal stop and that *sq, *ʃq and *ɬq collapsed into ejective fricatives. The evidence comes from one language.
